note.specFocus: Jesus' teaching on divorce, and how Catholic and Protestant attitudes to divorce and remarriage differ.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
2.6 Divorce and Remarriage
Jesus' own teaching on marriage's permanence creates an important tension for Christians facing divorce and remarriage.
Jesus' teaching on divorce
• Mark 10:2–9 records Jesus teaching that marriage is intended by God to be permanent, concluding: "what God has joined together, let no one separate."
• Matthew 19:9 includes an exception clause permitting divorce in the case of sexual immorality (porneia), which different denominations interpret more or less strictly.
Denominational differences on divorce
• The Catholic Church generally does not recognise divorce; a Catholic marriage is considered indissoluble, so the Church instead offers annulment, a declaration that a valid sacramental marriage never actually existed (for example due to a serious defect in consent).
• Many Protestant churches permit divorce, particularly in cases of adultery, abuse or irretrievable breakdown, emphasising God's forgiveness and the pastoral reality of human failure.
Remarriage
• The Catholic Church typically will not remarry a divorced person in church while a former spouse is alive, unless an annulment has been granted.
• The Church of England changed its policy in 2002, allowing remarriage of divorcees in church at the discretion of the local vicar — a significant pastoral shift balancing the ideal of lifelong marriage with compassion for those who have experienced breakdown.
• Most other Protestant churches are generally willing to bless remarriage, stressing grace, forgiveness and the possibility of a fresh start.
Exam link: "Choose one religion" questions on remarriage reward naming a specific denominational policy (e.g. Catholic annulment, Church of England's 2002 change) rather than a vague "Christians have mixed views".

questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Jesus taught in Mark 10:2–9 that marriage is intended by God to be a permanent union, concluding "what God has joined together, let no one separate"; many Christians, especially the Catholic Church, use this teaching to oppose divorce and instead offer annulment in certain limited circumstances.

2. Many Protestant churches permit divorce, particularly where there has been adultery, abuse or the irretrievable breakdown of a marriage, emphasising God's forgiveness and the pastoral need to allow people a fresh start rather than treating every divorce as sinful.
questions.question: Choose one religion. Outline two attitudes to divorce.

questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, The Catholic Church generally does not recognise remarriage in church while a former spouse is still alive, because it holds that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; a Catholic seeking to remarry in church would normally need to obtain an annulment, which declares that no valid marriage existed in the first place.

Second, The Church of England changed its policy in 2002 so that, at the discretion of the local vicar, divorced people may be remarried in church, reflecting a pastoral balance between upholding the ideal of lifelong marriage and recognising human failure and the possibility of a fresh start.

Finally, Many other Protestant churches are generally more willing to bless remarriage, especially where the first marriage ended through circumstances such as adultery or abuse, emphasising God's grace and the belief that people should not be permanently excluded from marriage because of past breakdown.

questions.examTip: Use accurate Christian teaching, explain why each point matters, and in an evaluation compare arguments before reaching a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of forgiveness, permanence of marriage, pastoral care and denominational differences and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
